title: Embeddings & Semantic Similarity
summary: Retrieval by meaning needs a way to compare meaning numerically. An embedding model maps text to a high-dimensional vector so that passages with similar meaning land near each other in that space. You measure 'near' with cosine similarity — the angle between two vectors — which is why 'car' and 'automobile' score high even though they share no letters. Embeddings are the mathematical substrate that makes semantic search, and therefore RAG retrieval, possible.

subtopics.title: Text becomes a vector
subtopics.explanation: An embedding model reads a string and outputs a fixed-length list of floats — a point in a high-dimensional space — where the geometry encodes meaning learned from huge text corpora. The exact numbers are opaque, but their relative positions are meaningful. Turning text into vectors is the first move that lets you do math on meaning at all.
subtopics.example:
# An embedding model maps any text to the same-length vector
def embed(text):
    # real models return e.g. 1536 floats; toy version here
    return MODEL.encode(text)

v_dog = embed("a puppy playing in the yard")
v_car = embed("a sedan parked in the driveway")
print(len(v_dog), len(v_car))  # e.g. 384 384 -- same fixed dimension

subtopics.title: Similar meaning lands nearby
subtopics.explanation: Because the model is trained so that texts used in similar contexts get similar vectors, semantically related passages cluster together even with no shared words. 'How do I reset my password?' sits near 'I forgot my login credentials'. This proximity-equals-meaning property is exactly what lets retrieval find relevant passages that keyword search would miss.
subtopics.example:
queries = [
    "how do I reset my password",
    "I forgot my login credentials",   # near: same intent, no shared words
    "what time does the store open",    # far: unrelated meaning
]
vecs = [embed(q) for q in queries]
# vecs[0] and vecs[1] are close; vecs[2] is distant

subtopics.title: Cosine similarity measures closeness
subtopics.explanation: Cosine similarity is the cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1.0 means same direction (very similar), 0 means unrelated, negative means opposing. It ignores vector length and cares only about direction, which is ideal for text where you want meaning, not magnitude. Cosine is the standard score every vector store uses to rank retrieval results.
subtopics.example:
import numpy as np

def cosine(a, b):
    a, b = np.array(a), np.array(b)
    return float(a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b)))

a = [1.0, 0.0, 1.0]
b = [1.0, 0.0, 0.9]   # nearly same direction
c = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]   # orthogonal -> unrelated
print(round(cosine(a, b), 3))  # ~0.997
print(round(cosine(a, c), 3))  # 0.0

subtopics.title: Embedding models and how you use them
subtopics.explanation: You pick a dedicated embedding model (hosted API or open-source) and must embed both your stored passages and every incoming query with the same model, since vectors from different models aren't comparable. Query and document vectors then live in one shared space where cosine ranks them. Choosing and consistently applying one embedding model is what makes stored and query vectors line up for retrieval.
subtopics.example:
# One model for BOTH sides -- never mix models
EMBED = load_model("text-embedding-3-small")

# index time: embed every stored chunk
chunk_vecs = [EMBED.encode(c) for c in chunks]

# query time: embed the query with the SAME model
q_vec = EMBED.encode("reset my password")
scores = [cosine(q_vec, cv) for cv in chunk_vecs]  # comparable space

subtopics.title: Dimensions and the trade-offs
subtopics.explanation: The vector length (e.g. 384, 768, 1536) is the model's dimensionality: more dimensions can capture finer distinctions but cost more memory and compute to store and search. Higher-dimension embeddings usually retrieve a bit better but make your index larger and queries slower. Picking a dimension is a quality-versus-cost decision that directly shapes the vector store you'll build next.
subtopics.example:
# Same text, two models of different dimensionality
small = embed_384("quarterly revenue report")   # 384 dims
large = embed_1536("quarterly revenue report")   # 1536 dims

# storage scales with dims x #chunks x 4 bytes (float32)
n_chunks = 1_000_000
print(384 * n_chunks * 4 / 1e9, "GB")    # ~1.5 GB
print(1536 * n_chunks * 4 / 1e9, "GB")   # ~6.1 GB -- 4x the memory

foundations.overview: Semantic retrieval requires comparing meaning as numbers, and embeddings are how that is done: an embedding model maps any text to a fixed-length vector in a high-dimensional space that it learned so that texts with similar meaning end up geometrically close, even when they share no words. You compare two vectors with cosine similarity — the cosine of the angle between them — which ranges from 1 (same direction, very similar) through 0 (unrelated) to negative (opposing) and deliberately ignores magnitude so only direction, i.e. meaning, matters. Crucially, both your stored passages and every incoming query must be embedded with the same model so their vectors share one comparable space; retrieval then ranks stored vectors by cosine to the query vector. The model's dimensionality (often 384 to 1536) trades retrieval quality against memory and search cost, a decision that directly sizes the vector index you build later. Embeddings plus cosine similarity are the mathematical substrate beneath every dense retriever in RAG.
foundations.formalDefinition: An embedding is a learned function that maps text to a fixed-dimensional real-valued vector such that semantic similarity between texts corresponds to a distance/similarity metric (commonly cosine similarity) between their vectors. Cosine similarity of vectors a and b is (a · b) / (||a|| ||b||), the cosine of the angle between them.
foundations.whyItMatters: Keyword matching fails when users phrase things differently from the source ('forgot password' vs 'reset credentials'). Embeddings let retrieval match on meaning, which is what makes RAG able to surface the right passage regardless of wording — the single most important ingredient in dense retrieval quality.
foundations.mentalModel: Imagine every sentence pinned as a dot on a giant map where directions mean topics: all the 'password/login' sentences cluster in one region, all the 'store hours' sentences in another. Cosine similarity is asking 'do these two dots point the same way from the center?' — closer angle, closer meaning.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Semantic search over docs, deduplication and clustering, recommendation, near-duplicate detection, and the retrieval step of essentially every production RAG system, where query and chunk embeddings are compared by cosine.
commonUseCases: Semantic search that matches meaning, not keywords
Ranking retrieved chunks by cosine similarity in RAG
Recommendation by nearest neighbors in embedding space

commonMisconceptions.myth: Higher cosine similarity always means the passage answers the question.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Cosine measures topical/semantic closeness, not whether the passage contains the answer. A closely related but unhelpful chunk can still score high — retrieval ranking is a signal, not a guarantee.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can mix embeddings from different models.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Vectors from different models live in different spaces and are not comparable. You must embed queries and documents with the same model (and version) for cosine scores to mean anything.
More dimensions can capture finer meaning but cost more memory and slower search, with diminishing returns. Dimensionality is a quality-versus-cost trade-off, not 'bigger wins'.

checkpoints.prompt: Two texts share no words but describe the same idea. Why can embeddings still rank them as similar?
options: The model maps meaning to vector direction, so same-meaning texts point the same way
They are compared by string length
It only works if they share at least one word
checkpoints.explanation: Embedding models are trained so that semantically related texts get vectors pointing in similar directions, regardless of shared words. Cosine similarity then scores that directional closeness high.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this print (cosine of two orthogonal vectors)?
checkpoints.explanation: The vectors are perpendicular, so their dot product is 0 and cosine similarity is 0.0. Note magnitude (the 5) is divided out — cosine ignores length and measures only direction.

checkpoints.prompt: You embedded your documents with model A. What must you use to embed incoming queries?
options: Any embedding model of the same dimension
A larger model for better quality
checkpoints.explanation: Vectors are only comparable within the space of the model that produced them. Even matching dimensions from a different model live in a different space, so you must embed queries with the same model A.

keyTakeaways: An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector where geometric proximity encodes semantic similarity, so meaning becomes math.
Cosine similarity — the cosine of the angle between two vectors — ranks closeness while ignoring magnitude, which is ideal for text.
Same-meaning texts score near 1.0 even with no shared words; that's why semantic search beats keyword matching for paraphrases.
Always embed queries and documents with the same model (and version); vectors from different models are not comparable.
Dimensionality (e.g. 384 vs 1536) trades retrieval quality against memory and search cost — a decision that sizes your vector index.
